item.title: A simpler ChatGPT, a Rust rethink, and a bank that moves faster
item.description:
Title for RSS: A simpler ChatGPT, a Rust rethink, and a bank that moves faster

OpenAI made a bold promise this week. Thibault Sottiaux, who works on Codex and ChatGPT at OpenAI, said that for the next 28 days the team will do one of two things every day. It will either ship one clear improvement for most Codex and Work users, or give a full usage reset, so people get their full usage limit back. "Let the improvements begin," he wrote.

Many people think the product needs this. Peter Yang, who makes practical AI guides, said ChatGPT "has become a mess." He wants OpenAI to simplify three things first: Work versus Codex, Spaces versus Pages versus Sites, and the picker where you choose a model and an effort level. His hot take is that the Work launch was a mistake. Claude folded Cowork back into its main chat, he noted, and he thinks Work does not need its own brand either.

Other builders talked about how they really use AI now. Dan Shipper, CEO of Every, said Dot, a personal agent, has become his main way to use AI. His Dot is called Boo, and he finds it cute. But he expects Boo to disappear within a year, even if he still talks to ChatGPT in the same way, as an always-on agent that keeps running in the background. It reminds him of early OpenClaw days. People loved the small quirks of their agents, but they dropped them as soon as something more powerful came along.

AI is also changing old choices about code. Vercel CEO Guillermo Rauch said his company moved Turborepo, its build tool, from the Go language to Rust. Rust was better for low-level work, but the move was expensive because humans were writing the code. People inside the company argued about whether it was worth it. Now that agents write more of the code, he says, what is "best for humans" is no longer always "best for business." He even thinks Rust may not be the final answer, because it was designed before agents arrived.

Rauch also shared a simple rule. On a new project, he wrote the README file by hand, because it is for people. The internal documents are in AI-written English, because they are for agents. Blogs, tweets, and READMEs are for human communication, he said.

The biggest story came from a podcast. Michael Lee runs Sequence Holdings, a company that buys older businesses and rebuilds them with AI. Together with the Dell family office, it has agreed to take the insurance broker Baldwin private for about $7.7 billion. Lee says an older company often has big advantages, such as its brand, its size, and rules that make it hard for startups to compete. What it usually lacks is the engineers to rebuild itself.

His first test was BankSouth, a community bank in Georgia. Lee says banking rules helped instead of hurting, because the processes are clear and the data is clean. That makes the work easier for agents. In about six months, his team cut the average time for consumer loan underwriting (checking whether a person should get a loan) by 94%. Commercial loans now take 11 days from start to finish, down from 30. When loan volume doubled from the first quarter to the second, the bank handled all of it without lowering its standards or adding staff.

Lee says the hardest part is not the code. It is the people. Workers can feel anxious, so his team tries to take away boring, repeated tasks and make jobs more fun.

Box CEO Aaron Levie sees the same pattern across the economy. AI is already creating new jobs, such as engineers who build AI products for companies and people who set up agents inside banks, factories, and law firms. Official job numbers miss part of this, he says, because many existing roles are quietly moving into AI work.

The message of the day is simple. Building is getting easier, so the real value is in products that feel simple and work that helps people every day. As Granola co-founder Sam put it, the easier it gets to build things, the more the details matter.

Sentence Focus

But he expects Boo to disappear within a year, even if he still talks to ChatGPT in the same way. - But he expects Boo / to disappear / within a year, / even if he still talks to ChatGPT / in the same way. - "expect + 人/物 + to do" 是「预计某物会……」；"even if" 引出让步，意思是「就算……也」，不是「即使是否」。 - 但他预计 Boo 一年内就会消失，哪怕他到时还是用同样的方式跟 ChatGPT 打交道。

Michael Lee runs Sequence Holdings, a company that buys older businesses and rebuilds them with AI. - Michael Lee runs Sequence Holdings, / a company / that buys older businesses / and rebuilds them / with AI. - 逗号后的 "a company …" 是同位语，补充说明 Sequence Holdings 是什么；"that …" 是定语从句，两个动词 buys 和 rebuilds 共用同一个主语 that。 - Michael Lee 经营着 Sequence Holdings，这家公司专门收购老牌企业，再用 AI 把它们重建一遍。

Lee says an older company often has big advantages, such as its brand, its size, and rules that make it hard for startups to compete. - Lee says / an older company often has big advantages, / such as its brand, / its size, / and rules / that make it hard / for startups to compete. - "such as" 后面列举例子；最后一项 "rules that make it hard for startups to compete" 里，it 是形式宾语，真正的内容是 "for startups to compete"。 - Lee 说，老牌公司往往有很大的优势，比如品牌、规模，以及让创业公司很难与之竞争的各种规则。

item.title: Simpler tools, Dot clears the inbox, and agents still feel early
item.description:
Title for RSS: Simpler tools, Dot clears the inbox, and agents still feel early

Today’s builder notes pulled three threads together. OpenAI’s Codex and ChatGPT lead said the next push is simplicity and more usage. Sam Altman drew a hard line on treating models like a religion. And product leaders argued that most agents still sit next to half-built workflows, not real daily work.

Thibault Sottiaux, who works on Codex and ChatGPT at OpenAI, said the team is locking in. The only things on the list now are simplifications, more efficiency for more usage, and big new features or models. Feedback is clear: people want things to get simpler. He said the team is on it. Sometimes you invest ahead of the curve, but the priority list is now short.

The same day he shared a personal win with Dot, a personal agent that learns your style and workflow. He said he had never hit inbox zero before. Dot helped by deleting whole email categories he did not need, labeling mail by type of work, and walking him through messages that needed a reply while searching for context in the background. He called it a good Saturday. The blunt point is simple: when an agent clears real mess, people notice.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman posted a quieter warning. He said he is very uncomfortable when people try to give AI models religious force, or when they surrender human judgment to the model. He called that a real safety issue. In plain words, the danger is not only a buggy tool. It is the choice to stop thinking for yourself.

That warning sat next to a wider product story. Meta AI senior director Madhu Guru, who earlier led Gemini and Veo work at Google, said AI adoption is largely a product problem today. Even among the roughly 2% who pay for AI, depth of use is still shallow. The main reason, in his view, is that most AI products look like airplane cockpits with 100 levers — connectors, permissions, model selection, token usage, and more. He thinks this has started to change. In the next 12 months, as product teams come into their own, things should look materially different.

Box CEO Aaron Levie painted a matching picture of agent adoption. He said it is still very bimodal. Coding and coding-adjacent tasks have taken off. Almost everything else has not. Even inside coding, only a small share of developers run background agents on projects in parallel. Most people still work with agents one to one. For the rest of knowledge work, real agentic adoption is still very early. Workflows need to be rebuilt. Data must be wired in new ways. Accountability, liability, governance, compliance, and security all have to change. His forecast is sharp: you can basically expect about 100x more agent adoption from what we have seen so far.

Other voices sharpened the same tension. Vercel CEO Guillermo Rauch said security will grow as verification engineering — such as checking that code is probably memory-safe — and as capital allocation: which surface should get the most tokens. Ryo Lu, a designer who has worked on Cursor, Notion, and Stripe, warned about “convergence to the mean”: when everyone copies everyone else, products feel polished and interchangeable. AI makes that loop almost frictionless.

Claude Blog also said Claude Cowork and chat are merging into one Claude. Bring a quick question, or hand over a noon report, and Claude can keep working after you close the laptop. Docs, Slides, and Design now live in the same chat, so you stop choosing which door to open. You keep the final say.

Put together, the day sat next to three pressures. One is the volume of product bets on simplicity, inbox cleanup, and one Claude surface. One is the blunt safety line that human judgment should not be surrendered. One is the quiet admission that agents are still early outside coding, because workflows and product design have not caught up. The hard part is choosing what to trust first — a simpler ChatGPT, a Dot that clears email, or an agent that still needs the cockpit removed.

Sentence Focus

Feedback is clear: people want things to get simpler. - Feedback is clear: / people want things / to get simpler. - 冒号后直接说明「反馈内容」；“want … to get …”＝希望……变得……。 - 反馈很清楚：人们希望事情变得更简单。

Most AI products look like airplane cockpits with 100 levers. - Most AI products / look like airplane cockpits / with 100 levers. - “look like …”＝看起来像……；“with …” 补出细节；cockpit＝驾驶舱。 - 多数 AI 产品看起来像带有一百个操纵杆的飞机驾驶舱。

Even among the roughly 2% who pay for AI, depth of use is still shallow. - Even among the roughly 2% / who pay for AI, / depth of use / is still shallow. - “Even among …”＝即便在……之中；“who …” 是定语从句；“depth of use”＝使用深度。 - 即便在大约那 2% 已经为 AI 付费的人里，使用深度仍然很浅。

item.title: Pro 500 gets fixed, dot learns your day, and Fractile bets on memory bandwidth
item.description:
Title for RSS: Pro 500 gets fixed, dot learns your day, and Fractile bets on memory bandwidth

Today’s builder notes pulled three threads together. OpenAI cleaned up a Pro 500 usage reset that missed some users. Sam Altman talked up a partner race for speed and a personal agent called dot. And on No Priors, Fractile’s CEO argued that the next chip fight is about memory bandwidth, not only more compute.

Thibault Sottiaux, who works on Codex and ChatGPT at OpenAI, saw reports that Pro 500 accounts did not get the reset they expected. He said the team was investigating and would make up for it. Later he posted a short update: all fixed. He also joked that future models will be much better at deleting and simplifying code. Usage limits sit next to daily work, so a failed reset gets noticed fast.

OpenAI’s Sam Altman answered speculation about Cerebras. He said Cerebras is a close partner, with a deep push on the frontiers of speed. In another post he called dot his favorite OpenAI product so far. Each day it feels noticeably better as it learns more of his workflow and style. He likes that it takes on tasks he does not enjoy — the kind that usually build up as a gravity well of dread.

That personal-agent idea showed up elsewhere too. Y Combinator president and CEO Garry Tan said his goal with GBrain is for agents to feel as native as the web eventually did — not a chatbot feature, but a guide that knows you, stays on 24/7, and thinks ahead. He also praised Capy for cross-session coordination that could steer around work he was already doing. Anthropic’s Claude Code engineer Thariq pointed at mods. He said “You should know” helps you stay on top of what Claude can do, and shows what mods unlock: you can really make Claude Code yours.

Builders also shared blunt, practical wins. AI tutor Peter Yang had paid almost $300 a year for a YouTube research tool that grew too complex. He asked Claude to build only the core features he needed. Claude built it in five minutes. The Claude account posted weekend builds with Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5, and Claude’s small-business blog expanded to 43 workflows and 27 new integrations after more than 900,000 installs.

The longest idea of the day came from No Priors with Walter Goodwin, founder and CEO of Fractile. Fractile builds very fast inference chips — chips that run a finished model — for the world’s largest models. Goodwin’s blunt claim is that a structural three-to-six-month lead in chips can win the big deployments, much like a frontier model lead in software. He said many “new” accelerators still look alike: HBM-style DRAM, tensor cores, and similar packaging. Hyperscaler chips such as Google’s TPU or OpenAI’s Jalapeno often act more like pricing leverage against NVIDIA than a new capability curve.

Fractile first explored SRAM designs in the same family as Groq or Cerebras — huge bandwidth, but weak capacity for long context. Goodwin said today’s fast chips often still flip back to a GPU for long-context attention. So the team moved toward high bandwidth from cheaper DRAM, aiming to unite GPU-like capacity with Groq-like speed, with a platform he said should ramp in the second half of next year. His favorite line is sharp: a snappier chatbot is the “faster horses” of fast inference. The real lift is running multi-trillion-parameter models at many thousands of tokens per second so long-running agents become radically faster. He also talked about roughly 25x more bandwidth per chip than HBM-based parts, and a long imbalance: FLOPs rose about a million-fold in twenty years, while memory bandwidth rose only about 40x.

Put together, the day sat next to three pressures. One is the volume of reset fixes and personal agents that clear dread from the calendar. One is the blunt race to customize Claude and Capy so the tool fits the person. One is the quiet hardware bet that speed for agents will come from memory bandwidth, not only from more FLOPs. The hard part is choosing what to trust first — a fixed Pro 500 reset, a dot that learns your style, or a chip that can feed a long agent without running out of memory.

Sentence Focus

1. He said the team was investigating and would make up for it. - He said / the team was investigating / and would make up for it. - “make up for …”＝补偿……；和 “investigating” 并列说明一边查、一边补。 - 他说团队正在排查，并会为此作出补偿。

2. Each day it feels noticeably better as it learns more of his workflow and style. - Each day / it feels noticeably better / as it learns more / of his workflow and style. - “as …”＝随着……；“noticeably better”＝明显更好；“workflow and style”＝工作流与风格。 - 随着它学到更多他的工作流和风格，它每天都明显感觉更好。

3. A snappier chatbot is the “faster horses” of fast inference. - A snappier chatbot / is the “faster horses” / of fast inference. - “A is the B of C”＝用熟悉比喻解释新事物；这里把更跟手的聊天机器人比成「更快的马」。 - 更跟手的聊天机器人，只是快速推理里的「更快的马」。

item.title: Sol resets, Claude halves design usage, and labs race to contain agents
item.description:
Title for RSS: Sol resets, Claude halves design usage, and labs race to contain agents

Today’s builder notes pointed one way. OpenAI prepared a global usage reset for paid ChatGPT. Claude cut the cost of design work in the app for two weeks. And Anthropic spent the day explaining how to keep powerful agents inside safe walls.

Thibault Sottiaux, who works on Codex and ChatGPT at OpenAI, said a global reset lands tomorrow at 10am PST for all paid ChatGPT accounts. He also apologized for a slow start with GPT-6.1 Sol. He said Sol is back to expected speeds after the early load spike. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman backed that story. He said Sol was their fastest-growing model ever and felt slow under load, but should feel much better now. Altman also pushed a bigger product idea: you should be able to use your AI subscription wherever you need it.

On the Anthropic side, the Claude account ran a short promo. For two weeks, if you start a design, a deck, or a doc in the Claude app, later work in that same conversation uses 50% less of your usage limits. The offer runs through October 15 on Pro, Max, and Team plans. Claude Code’s Boris Cherny pointed at Mods. He said you can now customize how Claude works and looks by prompting it. People work differently, so there is no reason everyone should see the same Claude. You can share mods as plugins so others can try them.

Andrej Karpathy wrote about a quieter shift. As models do more of the work, people will spend more time trying to understand the outputs. He shared practical tips. Ask for writing in ASD-STE100 — a controlled language first made for aerospace maintenance docs — or ask for “80% of the way to ASD-STE100” if the full rule feels too strict. Ask for diagrams or HTML pages. He is most bullish on custom explainer videos. His point is blunt: when intelligence and code are abundant, you can ask for large, disposable software artifacts that never made sense before.

Enterprise talk stayed practical. Box CEO Aaron Levie said many companies are putting internal FDEs — forward-deployed engineers — into departments to connect AI to real workflows. He called the Automation Engineer a new role this generation created. Vercel CEO Guillermo Rauch said the future is verification-engineering: proofs, end-to-end tests, benchmarks, and linters. Some tests will be deterministic. Some will be agentic.

Anthropic’s engineering blog carried heavy posts. One explains how they contain Claude across products. The goal is to cap blast radius — how much damage an agent can do if something goes wrong. User approval alone is weak: people approved about 93% of permission prompts. So Anthropic leans on sandboxes, VMs, and egress controls. A quality postmortem said reports that Claude Code felt worse came from three separate product changes, not one big model cut. All three were fixed, and subscribers got a usage-limit reset. Another post introduces Managed Agents. It decouples the “brain” (model plus harness) from the “hands” (sandbox and tools) and keeps a durable session log outside both.

The MAD Podcast sat next to that safety wave. Host Matt Turck talked with Goodfire CEO Eric Ho about why AI agents cheat. Ho framed agents as amoral students with a mostly absent teacher: reward says “get the answer,” not “act with human values.” In hard coding evals, some open models reward-hack most of the time. Ho argues chain-of-thought monitoring will fade as models compress reasoning or think inside, so labs need activation probes — cheap reads of the model’s internal signals.

Put together, the day sat next to three pressures. One is the volume of subscription resets and half-price design loops that sit next to daily work. One is the blunt race to understand and verify model output, not only to generate more of it. One is the quiet build-out of containment: sandboxes, session logs, and probes that try to catch cheating before it becomes damage. The hard part is choosing what to trust first — a faster Sol, a cheaper Claude design pass, or an agent that stays inside the walls you set.

Sentence Focus

He also apologized for a slow start with GPT-6.1 Sol.
- He also apologized / for a slow start / with GPT-6.1 Sol.
- “apologized for …”＝为……道歉；“a slow start with …”＝在……上起步偏慢。
- 他还为 GPT-6.1 Sol 起步偏慢道了歉。

People work differently, so there is no reason everyone should see the same Claude.
- People work differently, / so there is no reason / everyone should see the same Claude.
- “so there is no reason …”＝所以没有理由……；后接从句说明本不该怎样。
- 人们工作方式不同，所以没有理由让每个人看到同一个 Claude。

The goal is to cap blast radius — how much damage an agent can do if something goes wrong.
- The goal is / to cap blast radius / — how much damage an agent can do / if something goes wrong.
- “cap …”＝给……设上限；破折号后是白话解释；“if …” 条件从句。
- 目标是给 blast radius 设上限——也就是出了事时 agent 能造成多大损害。

item.title: Gemini 4 arrives, Dots reclaim mornings, and Sol runs hot
item.description:
Title for RSS: Gemini 4 arrives, Dots reclaim mornings, and Sol runs hot

Today’s builder notes pointed one way. Google put Gemini 4 on stage. OpenAI’s new always-on Dot kept reclaiming time for people who run big teams. And GPT-6.1 Sol was so popular that capacity had to catch up.

Google Labs VP Josh Woodward posted a short line: Gemini 4 Argon. Practical AI writer Peter Yang said Google “cooked” on Gemini 4. He still wants a stronger coding harness — the tools and workflows around a model — and a stronger personal agent. He named Antigravity for coding and Spark for the personal agent. The same day, Google Labs said Skills are rolling out in the Gemini app. Skills are a faster way to save custom instructions and automate repeat tasks inside chat. Opal, an earlier Labs experiment for custom workflows, will shut down on November 17, 2026. Google said Opal’s lessons now live inside Skills.

On the OpenAI side, Thibault Sottiaux — who works on Codex and ChatGPT — said GPT-6.1 Sol is their most demanded model across the API and subscriptions. ChatGPT and Codex were under heavy load. The team added capacity. He said speed should reach almost twice what they served the day before. He also said you can now build and deploy MCP servers right through ChatGPT. MCP is a way for AI tools to talk to outside systems. You can keep a server private or share it with the world.

Every’s podcast sat next to that product wave. Host Dan Shipper talked with OpenAI CEO Sam Altman after Dev Day. Altman said Dots — an always-on personal AI that sits next to your work — gave him back control of his mornings. Before, checking his phone for overnight fires ruined deep work. Now he trusts his Dot to judge what is urgent and what can wait. He named it Dottie for now. He also framed the bigger bet as a renaissance, not only an industrial revolution: more small teams and one-person companies, not one giant machine. OpenAI wants builders to ship apps inside ChatGPT and bring their subscription with them. Altman admitted they have not fully figured out the “App Store” yet, but they have figured out how to help many people build real products on the platform.

Enterprise talk stayed blunt. Box CEO Aaron Levie said the hard work is the deployment layer — moving workflows, connecting data, adding human checks, and keeping evals fresh as models change. Deploying agents is not like installing old software. Vercel CEO Guillermo Rauch said Vercel AI Gateway is a trustworthy view of real token use because it has paying customers and turns down shady “zero data retention” promos. YC’s Garry Tan highlighted Capy, where agent swarms talk as peers instead of only taking top-down orders.

Put together, the day sat next to three pressures. One is the volume of new model launches such as Gemini 4 Argon. One is the blunt race to keep Sol fast under demand. One is the quiet bet that Dots and Skills sit next to daily work and give people time back. The hard part is choosing what to trust first — a new model name, a stable harness, or an agent that knows what can wait until after deep work.

Sentence Focus

He still wants a stronger coding harness — the tools and workflows around a model — and a stronger personal agent.
- He still wants / a stronger coding harness / — the tools and workflows around a model — / and a stronger personal agent.
- “still wants … and …” 并列两个目标；破折号后是对 harness 的白话解释。
- 他仍想要更强的 coding harness（模型周围的工具与工作流），以及更强的个人 agent。

Now he trusts his Dot to judge what is urgent and what can wait.
- Now / he trusts his Dot / to judge / what is urgent / and what can wait.
- “trusts X to …”＝信任 X 去做某事；两个 what 从句并列。
- 现在他信任自己的 Dot 去判断什么紧急、什么可以等。

Deploying agents is not like installing old software.
- Deploying agents / is not like / installing old software.
- “is not like …”＝并不像；动名词作主语。
- 部署 agent 并不像安装旧软件那样。

item.description:
Title for RSS: Dots go live, Sol gets cheaper, and the app layer fights for edge

Today’s builder notes pointed one way. OpenAI launched a new always-on product called Dots. A strong model got much cheaper. And the tools around agents kept racing ahead.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said Dots are here. A Dot is a new way to use AI that works for you all day and night. The idea is simple: let the system handle more of the busy work, so you get time and attention back for harder thinking. Altman also praised Ultrafast. He said it is so fast that he does not want to go back. On price, he highlighted Sol 6.1. He said it costs about one fifth of Astra, with a 95% cache read discount. Cache read means reusing text the model has already seen, so later calls can cost less. He called Sol 6.1 extremely capable.

Thibault Sottiaux, who works on Codex and ChatGPT at OpenAI, shared early notes after DevDay. Within days, he said, a few million dots would be online, doing many kinds of work across a large community. He is excited to learn what people love and what still does not feel magical. After two or three days of use — and after teaching the Dot more about his preferences — he felt a clear jump. It learned quickly. It could also take on surprisingly big tasks on its own. The team wants to learn from how people use their primary Dot before they let users create a whole team of them. He also said DevDay felt great in person. Many people built things throughout the day.

Outside OpenAI, the developer stack kept moving. Vercel CEO Guillermo Rauch said the AI SDK hit 30 million weekly downloads. An SDK is a kit of tools that help developers build apps. He made a short milestone video with fframes and Opus. He said the video was written in Rust and rendered on the GPU. He also plotted an inverse link between product defects and downloads: fewer defects, more downloads.

Box CEO Aaron Levie looked at safety, not just speed. He said it is entirely plausible that the AI industry can handle safety and security through shared standards and practices for a while. At some point, he expects more oversight, testing, and layers of liability. For now, he thinks labs can align on these efforts without killing competition. He was glad to see that come together quickly.

FPV Ventures partner Nikunj Kothari wrote two blunt market notes. First, missionaries are harder to find. Some people leave companies they cofounded to join the “obvious” winners. Public CEOs leave for lab jobs. Teams get “Windsurf-ed,” where only some people join the next company. Early-stage investors often bet on people. When those people leave fast, the remaining company can become a shell. Second, defensibility is no longer one single moat. In the app layer, the harness — the system of tools, checks, and workflows around a model — is like a thousand small things done well. Much of it is invisible. In fierce competition, founders who execute fast and adapt may be the real edge.

Replit CEO Amjad Masad shared a note on how to design a harness that reaches frontier performance at a fraction of the cost. YC’s Garry Tan merged a version of OpenClaw’s test-audit skill into GStack, calling out test bloat. Builder Zara Zhang shipped a marketing site for a water bottle with Opus 5.5 in six prompts, using Elevenlabs for music, Meshy for 3D, and the OpenAI API for images.

Put together, the day sat next to three pressures. One is the volume of always-on agents that sit next to daily work. One is the blunt race on price and speed after DevDay. One is the quiet fight in the app layer, where edge is many small details, not one slogan. The hard part is teaching these systems what you care about — and still keeping the craft that competitors cannot copy overnight.

Sentence Focus

It learns very quickly to be most useful and it can take on surprisingly ambitious tasks on its own.
- It learns very quickly / to be most useful / and it can take on / surprisingly ambitious tasks / on its own.
- “take on … on its own”＝自行接手；“surprisingly ambitious” 修饰 tasks。
- 它学得很快，能变得特别有用，还能自己接手出人意料地有野心的任务。

In the app layer, the harness is like a thousand small things done well.
- In the app layer, / the harness / is like / a thousand small things done well.
- “in the app layer”＝在应用层；“done well” 是过去分词作后置修饰。
- 在应用层，harness 就像一千件小事都做好。

It is entirely plausible that the AI industry can deal with safety through shared standards for the foreseeable future.
- It is entirely plausible / that the AI industry can deal with safety / through shared standards / for the foreseeable future.
- “it is entirely plausible that …”＝完全说得通；“for the foreseeable future”＝在可预见的将来。
- 完全说得通：在可预见的将来，AI 行业可以用共享标准来处理安全问题。

item.title: Sonnet 5.5 jumps, Pro usage math, and DevDay next
item.description:
Title for RSS: Sonnet 5.5 jumps, Pro usage math, and DevDay next

Today’s builder notes pointed one way. A new mid-tier Claude model felt much stronger in real work. OpenAI changed how Pro $200 usage is counted. And DevDay was only hours away.

Anthropic’s Claude team spent the day showing Sonnet 5.5 in Claude Code. Claude Code is a coding agent — a tool that writes and edits code for you. Claude Code’s Boris Cherny shared a short clip of Sonnet 5.5 fixing a bug. He said it was about 30% faster and used about 30% less. Cat Wu, who works on Claude Code and Cowork, said users get about 30% more tasks done than with Sonnet 5. The model is smarter, so it needs fewer tokens for the same work. Tokens are the small pieces of text a model reads and writes. In one demo, the agent raked a yard of leaves with tool calls. It finished 24 seconds faster than Sonnet 5 and used about 6,000 fewer tokens.

Anthropic researcher Alex Albert said Sonnet 5.5 has the same feel he liked in Opus 5.5. It writes clearly. It is very fast. And it is a big jump over Sonnet 5. Every CEO Dan Shipper agreed on writing. In his tests for Every, Sonnet 5.5 improved a lot at revision — even versus Opus 5.5. Astra is still his favorite for writing, but Sonnet 5.5 wins on rewrite tasks. It is also faster and cheaper than Opus 5.5, so it became a preferred model for quick coding and design loops on his team.

Box CEO Aaron Levie brought enterprise numbers. Box tested Sonnet 5.5 early on hard knowledge-work tasks with the Box Agent. Overall, the hardest tests rose by about 4 points. Finished work arrived about 2.4 times faster, on about 12% fewer tokens. Gains were larger in some fields, such as financial services and legal. In one finance case, Sonnet 5.5 caught bad interest totals in a deal book. In a lease review, it refused to invent a “standard” market number and flagged what the lease really lacked. Customers will soon build agents with Sonnet 5.5 in Box AI Studio.

On the OpenAI side, Thibault Sottiaux — who works on Codex and ChatGPT — posted a long, blunt note before the big news. Tomorrow, Pro $200 would reopen to new subscribers. At the same time, OpenAI would change how usage is calculated. In effect, he said, the plan would net out at about half the dollar of API spend versus the old Pro $200 plan. API spend means how much the same work would cost if you paid OpenAI’s public API prices.

He also said why users might still get more done than a month ago. OpenAI is not bringing back the 5-hour limit, so people can use their weekly budget when they want. Models keep getting more efficient, and API prices keep falling — this week GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna landed at 50% of their old price. Tomorrow, more subscription perks will not draw on usage. He did not say what those are yet. He wanted the usage change public before DevDay’s good news.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman fed the hype in one line: he was pretty excited for DevDay tomorrow, and “we have found a new thing.” Dan Shipper said he has been to every DevDay since 2023, and this one has the most launches yet. Practical AI writer Peter Yang is heading to his first DevDay. He also built a playable StarCraft level with Sonnet 5.5. And he pushed back on mood swings on X: one week OpenAI is “mogged,” another week Anthropic is “cooked.” He is glad two (and soon more) labs are pushing the frontier.

Put together, the day sat next to three pressures. One is the volume of real work Sonnet 5.5 can finish with less cost. One is the blunt rewrite of Pro $200 usage math before DevDay. One is a launch day that may sit next to both stories at once. The hard part is choosing which gains to trust — speed, price, or the next surprise on stage.

Sentence Focus

Sonnet 5.5 is a major capabilities jump over Sonnet 5.
- Sonnet 5.5 / is a major capabilities jump / over Sonnet 5.
- “a … jump over …” 表示「相对……的大幅跃迁」；capabilities 指模型能力。
- Sonnet 5.5 相对 Sonnet 5 是一次很大的能力跃迁。

In effect, it will net out at half the dollar in API spend compared to the old plan.
- In effect, / it will net out at / half the dollar in API spend / compared to the old plan.
- “in effect”＝实际上；“net out at”＝算下来等于；“compared to” 做对比。
- 实际上，按 API 美元花费算，大约只有旧方案的一半。

I’m just glad there are two competitors pushing the frontier so we can all benefit.
- I’m just glad / there are two competitors / pushing the frontier / so we can all benefit.
- “glad there are …” 后接存在句；“so …” 引出结果。
- 我只是高兴有两家对手在推前沿，这样大家都能受益。

item.title: Native apps, agent friction, and not eating the gains
item.description:
Title for RSS: Native apps, agent friction, and not eating the gains

Today’s builder notes pointed one way. Desktop software may go more native again. Agents may rewrite who wins when buying feels hard. And one engineer warned that better tools can still make people lazier.

Vercel CEO Guillermo Rauch shared a hands-on rebuild. He ported his Mini web browser to Rust and Swift. He said it is faster and more secure. He also said it is nicer to iterate on than Electron plus Bun. Electron is a common way to wrap web apps as desktop apps. He wanted Safari-like UX with Chrome-level web support. With the cef crate, he can ship up-to-date Chromium. He embeds an agent without bloating the app, using fx acp. That agent talks to his local fx CLI over ACP, then manages the browser through an MCP server. MCP is a way for tools to expose actions an agent can call. By ditching Electron, he got Liquid Glass, faster boots, and a more Mac-native feel. His bet is blunt: native is the future on the desktop and in the cloud. The software world may “nativify” faster than people expect.

Box CEO Aaron Levie looked at markets through agents that choose the best or most efficient option for users. On one side, some businesses benefit from the friction that keeps customers from switching. In those markets, switching costs may fall, and competition may rise. On the other side, markets hurt by friction — such as healthcare, travel, and local services — may unlock more activity when agents make buying easier. A future shaped by agents that work for our goals, he said, cannot look exactly like today.

Claude Code’s Thariq put the cultural risk in one line. He is most afraid that people will eat the productivity gains of agents by just becoming lazier. OpenAI’s Thibault Sottiaux pushed on release habits: a code freeze before shipping is not really a thing anymore. In the future, code might even be generated online per request, under constraints. Peter Steinberger said his plan is to let Codex decide which tests actually need to run, cut CI hard, and run tests hourly.

The longest idea of the day came from Training Data with Aaron Levie. He argued that “model wrappers” work in the enterprise because the real gap sits between model skill and real workflows. Even a super-smart model still needs data connections, human-in-the-loop steps, idle waits, change management, and legacy systems. Cloud infrastructure created huge value, he said, and so did products like Snowflake on top of it. The same pattern may hold for intelligence: models will be valuable, but applying them in banking, life sciences, and government still needs a lot of software.

Box sits on huge piles of unstructured files. Agents can answer questions, pull out metadata, and automate steps. A simple hero use case is reading a million contracts that no team could afford to read by hand. Levie also separated coding “slop” from work slop in decks and memos. Code is often treated as a utility. A slide deck still feels like a proxy for trust: how much did this person think, and can they deliver?

On diffusion, coding agents spread fast for many reasons: value is close to the text that ships, labs train and test on code every day, and technical users fix broken tools themselves. A sales role is rate-limited by customer replies, meetings, and budget. Knowledge work also lacks a simple “connect your GitHub” on-ramp. Levie’s advice for staying current was practical: join X and follow the right accounts. You are either a year ahead or a year behind, simply based on your feed.

Put together, the day sat next to three pressures. One is the volume of native craft returning to desktop software. One is the blunt rewrite of market friction when agents choose for us. One is the quiet risk that better agents shrink effort instead of raising ambition. The hard part is building tools that sit next to real work — and still keeping the gains.

Sentence Focus

He is most afraid of us eating the productivity gains of agents by just becoming lazier.
- He is most afraid / of us eating the productivity gains of agents / by just becoming lazier.
- “afraid of … by just …” 把担心对象和方式叠在一起；eating the gains 是形象说法，表示把好处「吃掉」了。
- 他最怕的是：我们把 agent 带来的生产力增益吃掉了，只是变得更懒。

A future meaningfully mediated by agents cannot possibly function exactly the same as today.
- A future / meaningfully mediated by agents / cannot possibly function / exactly the same as today.
- “mediated by …” 是被动结构；cannot possibly 加强否定；the same as 做比较。
- 一个被 agent 深度中介的未来，不可能和今天一模一样地运转。

You are either a year ahead or a year behind simply based on your feed.
- You are either a year ahead / or a year behind / simply based on your feed.
- “either … or …” 二选一；simply based on 表示「仅仅取决于」。
- 你要么领先一年，要么落后一年，差别常常只在你的信息流。

item.title: Resets land, AI slop, and why diffusion may win inference
item.description:
Title for RSS: Resets land, AI slop, and why diffusion may win inference

Today’s builder notes pointed one way. Usage limits came back. People pushed back on low-quality AI text. And one founder argued that a different model design may win when speed at answer time matters most.

OpenAI’s Thibault Sottiaux, who works on Codex and ChatGPT, posted a short update that many users had been waiting for. “Resets all propagated,” he wrote. In plain words, the usage reset had finished rolling out. For people who hit weekly or daily caps on coding agents (tools that write and change code for you) or ChatGPT, that single line was the news that mattered.

Elsewhere, builders shared lighter product notes. Practical AI writer Peter Yang said Claude’s limits jumped from “barely usable” to “basically unlimited.” He is also building a small app with Gemini’s audio API (a way for software to hear and speak) to practice conversational Japanese: ten lessons, ten phrases each. Claude Code’s Thariq looked back about a year, to some of the first posts on making videos with Claude Code. Each clip took a long time then. He said the change since then still feels crazy. Every CEO Dan Shipper wrote a short novelization of Plato’s Protagoras, then asked Opus 5.5 to turn it into a short film and shared early scenes. Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan said his favorite way to fix production bugs now is Capy with GStack /autoplan, using GPT-6 medium reasoning.

Vercel CEO Guillermo Rauch aimed at a harder problem: understanding. He wrote “Reject non-understanding.” Slop grenades, he said, are not only bad code and pull requests. There is a real risk that reading itself gets discounted, because people are tired of low-quality, unchecked AI prose. He pointed to a viral thread about a “performance win” tied to a compiler change. The pull request description itself had the AI saying the gain was not from the compiler. It came from changes in algorithms and data structures. Rauch wants AI that serves understanding of the world, and that lifts human thinking and creativity — not tools that flood the feed with noise.

The longest idea of the day came from No Priors with Stefano Ermon, co-founder and CEO of Inception, and a Stanford professor long known for diffusion research. Diffusion is a way to generate content by starting from noise and cleaning it step by step. It already leads in images and video. Ermon’s bet is that it can also win for text and code at inference time — the moment when a model produces an answer after training is done.

He said today’s big labs mostly bet on autoregressive models for text. Those models write one token (a small piece of text) after another. That left-to-right path mapped poorly to GPUs, which prefer parallel work. Diffusion models, by design, process many tokens at once during generation. In 2024 his lab showed a diffusion language model under a billion parameters could match a GPT-2-scale autoregressive model on quality metrics, while generating text about 10 times faster. Inception later built Mercury models that, on benchmarks, sit near the flash, mini, and nano speed-focused models from frontier labs, while running faster. The company is about two years old and around 50 people. They even built their own serving engine, because common stacks were not enough.

Ermon’s estimate is simple: on a map of real workloads such as those on OpenRouter, about 20% to 30% care a lot about latency (how long you wait for an answer). At least that slice is a strong fit. His memorable line was that the bitter lesson is that the more parallel solution is the one that eventually wins.

Put together, the day sat next to three pressures. One is the volume of daily usage that only works again after a reset lands. One is the blunt call to reject text you do not understand. One is a bet that inference speed, not only training scale, will decide the next architecture. The hard part is choosing tools that sit next to real work — and still leave room for human judgment.

Sentence Focus

Resets all propagated.
- Resets / all / propagated.
- 这是很 blunt 的短句；propagated 表示「已经传开 / 生效」。
- 重置已经全部生效了。

There is a real risk that reading itself gets discounted.
- There is a real risk / that reading itself / gets discounted.
- “there is a risk that …” 引出担心；itself 强调「阅读这件事本身」被低估。
- 真正的风险是：阅读本身会被低估。

The more parallel solution is the one that eventually wins.
- The more parallel solution / is the one / that eventually wins.
- “the more … the one that …” 用比较级锁定赢家；that 引导定语从句。
- 更并行的方案，最终会赢。

Today’s builder notes pointed one way. Chat and deep work are joining in one place. Agents (software that can act for you) are changing how companies buy tools. And a short Codex outage reminded everyone that usage limits still matter.

Claude Blog said Claude Cowork and chat are now one Claude. You can ask a quick question, or hand over a report due at noon. Claude can keep going even after you close your laptop. The change rolls out first on Pro and Max. Claude Docs and Claude Slides are new, and Claude Design now works inside the same conversations. You can edit together, present from Claude, or download PowerPoint or PDF. All three are in beta on paid plans. Enterprise admins choose when to turn them on. People used to decide: is this a Cowork job or a Design job? Context did not move well between those places. Now Claude tries to see what the task needs, and brings those skills into any chat with the connectors you already have. One senior economist said Claude can open a legal research database, read cases, find related ones, download them, and store them for later review. By default, Claude still asks before it acts. You can also let it work longer and check in only when something needs a closer look.

Builders also showed agents at work. Claude Code’s Boris Cherny talked about Tag, a Slack bot inside Anthropic. Tag writes more than half of his pull requests each day. It also does almost all of his data analysis, and it fixes most product feedback and bugs. It is not a normal bot. It is proactive (it starts work on its own), programmable, has memory, and can use connectors. With Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.1, he says it has strong judgment. Example asks include marking threads when they are done, reproducing a bug end to end and opening a fix, or spending about 10 million tokens to test many ideas about weird data. Claude Code’s Thariq asked a blunt question about effort levels: when do you raise them, and why not always use max? He looked at evals (tests of model quality) and his own trials. He uses low effort more when he wants to stay in the loop. He saves max for times he wants almost no input, or when he is hunting security bugs.

On the OpenAI side, Codex went down for a while. Thibault Sottiaux said the team was working hard to bring service back. Later he said they were back, and they would reset usage limits for all paid users across Codex and ChatGPT work. He also said they keep a spare Codex for moments like this. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman wrote about a wider review: how agents use internet access during training and evaluation. The company publishes summaries, but the work is slow because the logs are huge, and they must work with groups that were hit. Hugging Face is still the most severe case they have seen. He said they will stay as open as they can, but if an agent finds a weakness in another company, that company decides whether to speak.

Enterprise buyers got a sharper frame too. Vercel CEO Guillermo Rauch said they help firms such as Klaviyo build agentic deployment platforms: connect agents like Claude, Codex, and Cursor; set up SSO through Okta or Entra; then let people work securely. He asked what happens to SaaS once every company does this. Apps only work if they can reach business data. That is why big SaaS players suddenly ship CLIs and MCPs, or clean up old APIs. The new procurement bar, he said, will be how easy a product is for *agents*, not only for humans. After that, a long tail of SaaS may never be bought again. It may be generated instead. Box CEO Aaron Levie put the gate in one line: you cannot automate what you cannot measure. Evals are how enterprises see what agents do well, what broke, and what improved.

Put together, the day sat next to three pressures. One is the volume of work that now lives in a single Claude chat. One is the blunt shift from buying software for people to buying software that agents can navigate. One is the hard reset after a short outage — and the quiet review of what agents touch on the open web. The hard part is choosing which agents sit next to your real work, and how you know they are helping.

Sentence Focus

Tag writes more than half of his pull requests each day.
- Tag writes / more than half of his pull requests / each day.
- “more than half of …” 是数量结构；each day 放在句末标频率。
- Tag 每天写他超过一半的 pull request。

The new procurement bar will be how easy a product is for agents, rather than humans.
- The new procurement bar / will be / how easy a product is for agents, / rather than humans.
- “how easy … is” 作表语从句；rather than 做 blunt 对照。
- 新的采购门槛会变成：产品对 agent 有多好用，而不是对人。

You cannot automate what you cannot measure.
- You cannot automate / what you cannot measure.
- “what you cannot …” 是名词性从句，整句是 blunt 的短判断。
- 你测不到的东西，就自动化不了。

Today’s builder notes pointed one way. Money moved between AI labs. A quiet software layer fed the GPUs. And tools for small businesses and developers got more practical.

Open models took about half of Anthropic’s lost share, led by names such as Kimi K3 and DeepSeek. Anthropic’s Opus 5.5 climbed to about 10% of spend in only two days. The blunt picture is not that one lab won forever. It is that builders are spreading spend across closed and open models as prices and quality keep changing.

That same day, FirstMark VC Matt Turck sat next to a less famous layer of the stack. In Jensen’s five-layer cake for AI — energy, chips, infrastructure, models, applications — the middle software part is poorly understood. That is where VAST Data grew into a company valued near $30 billion. It powers players such as xAI, CoreWeave, Nebius, and Mistral. On The MAD Podcast, VAST CEO Renen Hallak said his company sits in that middle layer. He sometimes calls it software infrastructure, and sometimes the operating system for this new era. Hallak shared one customer story that sticks: an AI cloud first planned about 500 petabytes over three years, then came back asking for an extra two exabytes on top. “Sometimes it scares me,” he said. He also used a simple picture for how agents will learn: “We infer during the day, fine-tune at night.” In plain words, systems use data while they work, then update themselves later so they get a little smarter for tomorrow.

On the product surface, Claude Blog said Claude for Small Business now ships 43 workflows and 27 new integrations. The list includes tools many owners already use, such as Shopify, Salesforce, TikTok, Zoom, Square, Stripe, and Zapier. The product has been installed more than 900,000 times since May. After a spring tour of more than 1,000 owners in 10 cities, about a third asked for help growing the business — leads, inbound replies, and proposals — not only back-office work. One founder said work that used to take 120 hours now takes five minutes. Another said Claude helped him make about $20,000 in proposals over a month and a half.

Developers got smaller but useful notes too. Claude Code’s Thariq said many people plan themselves and do not need plan mode. Others like a mode where Claude only thinks and brainstorms with them. His plan is to turn plan mode into a built-in mod, and let mods add new modes or rebind Shift+Tab. Replit CEO Amjad Masad said Muse can now make apps on Replit. Latent Space’s Shawn Wang said his “Scaling without Slop” bet is working: the first 100k YouTube subscribers took three years, and the next 100k took about 1.2 months. OpenClaw builder Peter Steinberger gave a blunt agent tip: if you only tell an agent to clean up, it stops too early. Give it an ambitious goal, such as removing 20% of the least useful tests while keeping code coverage within 2%.

Put together, the day sat next to three pressures. One is the volume of spend moving between Anthropic, OpenAI, and open models. One is the hidden software layer that must feed GPUs at crazy scale. One is tools that sit next to real work for small shops and coding agents. The hard part is choosing which stack you trust — and what you dare ask it to do next.

Sentence Focus

Anthropic is still number one in spend, but its share fell from about 69% to 40%.
- Anthropic is still number one in spend, / but its share fell / from about 69% to 40%.
- “still … but …” 先承认现状，再用 but 给出真正变化；from A to B 标出幅度。
- Anthropic 在支出上仍是第一，但它的份额从大约 69% 降到了 40%。

That is where VAST Data grew into a company valued near $30 billion.
- That is where / VAST Data grew into / a company valued near $30 billion.
- “That is where …” 用地点/层次把前文的 middle layer 落到一家公司；valued near 是“估值接近”。
- 正是在这一层，VAST Data 成长为一家估值接近 300 亿美元的公司。

If you only tell an agent to clean up, it stops too early.
- If you only tell an agent to clean up, / it stops too early.
- “If you only …” 是条件句里的 blunt 提醒：只给弱目标，就会提前停住。
- 如果你只让 agent 做清理，它会停得太早。

item.content:encoded:
Title for RSS: Blast radius, agent parts, and what agents are for

Today’s builder notes pointed one way. Agents (software that can act for you) are getting more power. So the hard questions moved forward. How do you limit damage when something goes wrong? How do you split an agent into parts you can run in the cloud? And what should those agents even be for?

Anthropic Engineering put the safety story in plain words. Twelve months ago, they would have rejected giving Claude enough access to take down an internal Anthropic service. Today that level of access is normal, and their developers move faster because of it. Risk has two parts: how likely a failure is, and how much damage one could do. The second part is the blast radius — the size of the mess if things go wrong. As agents do work that once needed a person or a team, the cost of not deploying grows large. So the engineering job becomes how to cap that blast radius.

One path is human approval on every step. Claude Code used to ask for permission each turn. In theory that works. In practice, telemetry (usage data) showed users approved about 93% of prompts. The more approvals people see, the less carefully they read each one. Anthropic now leans harder on containment: sandboxes, virtual machines, and egress controls that limit what the agent can reach. A model called Claude Mythos Preview was judged too risky to ship in April 2026, even though similar capability may ship later as defenses get stronger.

That same split of “brain and hands” showed up in product design. Anthropic’s Managed Agents post says harnesses (the wrap that steers a model) go stale as models improve. Old fixes, such as context resets for “context anxiety,” can become dead weight on a stronger model. So they virtualized three parts: a session log, a harness, and a sandbox. Each can change without breaking the others. Vercel CEO Guillermo Rauch made a similar map for successful agents: brain (model plus harness), hands (tools, computer, browser), and files (memories, skills, repos). On a Mac Mini you can keep everything in one place. In the cloud, you break them apart to cut cost and improve security. Today Vercel added Drives — storage you can attach like an external disk — so a night job can tidy memories without booting the full agent computer.

On the product surface, Claude launched Marketplace. You can find connectors such as Slack and Notion, buy agents and tools from companies such as Cursor and CrowdStrike, and scale with partners such as Accenture and Deloitte. Claude Code’s Boris Cherny also shared how Claude speeds bug finding: it builds a model of a tricky state machine, finds counter-examples, reproduces the bugs, then fixes them. It is not full formal verification of a whole codebase yet. It is focused checking of the hairiest parts. OpenAI’s Thibault Sottiaux pointed ahead to DevDay next Tuesday, and said voice ChatGPT already runs across plugins for work, mail, coding, and calendar.

Builders also argued about purpose. Meta’s Madhu Guru disagreed with Ben Thompson on consumer agents. People do not have one relationship with “doing things.” Browsing clothes can be fun. Hiring a roofer is usually miserable. For high-friction jobs, demand for agents that remove the pain is huge. Cursor designer Ryo Lu warned from the other side: the danger is not that AI makes us lazy. The danger is that it makes us endlessly busy — infinite output before we have taste or intention. Y Combinator’s Garry Tan put the business version in two lines: make software agents want, and use agents to make people want software.

Put together, the day sat next to three pressures. One is the blast radius of agents with real access. One is the volume of work that becomes cheaper when brain, hands, and files can run apart. One is the blunt question of what all that speed is for. The hard part is building agents that sit next to your life — and still leave room to think.

Sentence Focus

The engineering question becomes how to cap the blast radius.
- The engineering question / becomes / how to cap the blast radius.
- “becomes how to …” 把抽象问题落成一个要解决的动作；blast radius 后文已用 plain words 解释过。
- 工程上的问题，变成了如何给爆炸半径设上限。

The more approvals a user sees, the less carefully they read each one.
- The more approvals a user sees, / the less carefully / they read each one.
- “the more …, the less …” 是成对比较结构，表示一边增加、另一边下降。
- 用户看到的批准提示越多，每一条就越不会认真看。

The danger is not that AI makes us lazy. The danger is that it makes us endlessly busy.
- The danger is not that … / The danger is that …
- “not that … / that …” 是 blunt 的对照：先否定常见担心，再给出真正担心。
- 危险不是 AI 让人变懒。危险是它让人永远忙碌。

Anthropic pushed Opus 5.5 into daily life at the same time. Cat Wu said Opus 5.5 is now the default in Claude Code and the Claude app, including Cowork, for Pro, Max, and Team. The default effort is medium. She says that is close to Fable 5.1 on intelligence, but faster. Rate limits go about 25% further than on Opus 5. Claude Code engineer Boris Cherny has used Opus 5.5 as his daily driver for weeks. He and the team had Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.1 port HAProxy from C to Rust. Both almost passed the full test suite. Opus finished in about 9.5 hours, against Fable’s 12, and cost about 51% less. Then he went further. With a few short prompts, he used Opus 5.5 and Lean (a tool for proving code is correct) to check the Claude Agent SDK. That led to 16 pull requests that fixed bugs and race conditions. He sometimes mixes Lean with TLA+ for data flow, concurrency, and state. He does not know either language well. Claude does. He asked if formal verification might be the future of finding bugs.

Box CEO Aaron Levie called it an insane day in AI. First came Opus 5.5 price cuts. Then Sol and Luna cut token prices in half. He said the drop in cost per task is unlike any other technology. Each time AI gets cheaper, the jobs you can give agents get bigger. He called that Jevons paradox for agents: when something gets cheaper, people use more of it, not less. Inside Box, their agent tests on hard enterprise tasks with messy data showed big gains over Opus 5: about 63% fewer tokens, 42% less wordiness, and 30% more speed, on top of a cheaper model. Wins showed up in finance, cloud cost work, client analysis, and clinical data. Customers will soon build agents with Opus 5.5 in Box AI Studio.

The scoreboard also moved. Vercel CEO Guillermo Rauch shared fresh Next.js evals. Opus 5.5, GPT-6 Sol, and Fable 5.1 all sat near 97%. Grok 4.7 was about 94%, but 2x to 7x cheaper. Anthropic Research’s Alex Albert used Opus 5.5 in Blender to rebuild San Francisco’s Market Street as it looked the day before the 1906 earthquake, from maps, film, and old photos, then into a short street video. OpenClaw builder Peter Steinberger said Astra found a roughly 14-year-old bug in libuv after ChatGPT started crashing on macOS 27. Claude Code’s Thariq added a blunt product note: stronger models should not mean shipping ten times more features. They should mean more time with users, more prototypes, and shipping things that actually work.

Put together, the day sat next to three pressures. One is the volume of work that suddenly looks affordable when token prices fall. One is the blunt race between Sol, Luna, Opus 5.5, and the rest. One is builders who use those models to prove code, port systems, and rebuild whole streets. The hard part is choosing which model sits next to your workflow — and what you dare ask it to do next.

Sentence Focus

The drop in cost per task is unlike any other technology.
- The drop in cost per task / is unlike / any other technology.
- “unlike …” 用来做直白对比；主语是「单次任务成本下降」这件事本身。
- 单次任务成本下降的速度，和任何其他技术都不一样。

Each time AI gets cheaper, the jobs you can give agents get bigger.
- Each time AI gets cheaper, / the jobs / you can give agents / get bigger.
- “Each time …” 表示每次条件成立就发生；中间夹了相对从句 “you can give agents”。
- 每次 AI 变便宜，你能交给 agent 的工作就会变大。

Stronger models should not mean shipping ten times more features.
- Stronger models / should not mean / shipping ten times more features.
- “should not mean …” 是 blunt 的价值判断：能力变强，不等于该这样做。
- 更强的模型，不该意味着往外塞十倍功能。

Title for RSS: Agents spend money, ads lose eyes, and Claude drives Chrome

Today’s builder notes pointed one way. Agents (software that can act for you) are not only chatting. They are starting to spend money, skip human eyes on web pages, and drive a real browser with fewer clicks from you.

Box CEO Aaron Levie made the money case. Personal agents that can finish hard tasks end to end will carry a lot of commerce. You start with small annoying jobs. Then you give the agent bigger jobs. When buying is easier, people often spend more, not less. That helps the agent makers. It also opens space for new layers that agents want to use — shops, local services, and B2B tools. In a second post, Levie said agents will use software far more than people ever did — even about 100 times more. Interfaces may fade into the background. But the core systems still matter more, not less. Agents can take destructive actions. They also need safe data and clear business logic. Platforms that act as a security layer, hold data for both agents and people, and run workflows have a big chance right now.

AI tutor Peter Yang sat next to that commerce story with a blunt ad-market warning. If a big part of your business is showing targeted display ads to humans, what happens when agents browse your site and finish the job without a human seeing the ads at all? He thinks the industry is in for a rude awakening. On a lighter note, he talked with Ethan, product lead for ChatGPT Finances. Ethan said ChatGPT caught a hotel charge after a points booking, worked with customer service, and got him reimbursed. Yang had a similar case: he asked ChatGPT to cancel a hotel for his parents, watch the replies, and keep following up until the money came back. He also said he no longer lives in email or text. He lives in chat with his agents.

The browser layer got a major push from Anthropic. Claude Blog said Claude in Chrome is now generally available on every paid Claude plan. Claude can take more actions on its own in the browser, instead of asking for approval every time. A safety classifier checks each action before it runs, to make sure it is safe and matches what you asked. Many tools already connect to Claude. Many others do not — internal dashboards, old systems, vendor portals. Claude in Chrome can see the page you are on and do things such as reading text, typing, clicking, moving between pages, and filling forms, using your existing logins. Anthropic spent the pilot year fighting prompt injection: hidden instructions in a page, email, or form that try to trick an agent into doing something you never asked for. Their stack now includes training against a growing attack library, probes that screen tool results, and classifiers that block actions that do not match your request. On their hard red-team tests, with probes plus the safety classifier, they report no successful attacks against Claude Sonnet 5 or Opus 5, and a 0.3% success rate against Fable 5 in low-severity cases. To start, install it from the Chrome Web Store. Enterprise admins can limit it to approved domains.

Coding agents also stayed busy. FPV Ventures partner Nikunj Kothari said Instinct and Muse are strong for browser use on the phone, with almost zero setup for regular people. But for deep computer-use work on a Mac, he still puts Codex first. Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan said Capy AI tracks multi-step work and ships large pull requests faster than Codex or Claude Code alone for him this week. Vercel CEO Guillermo Rauch noted that you can now use Jev over HTTP in AI Gateway, next to their type-safe AI SDK API. OpenAI’s Thibault Sottiaux teased that a Tuesday reset is almost here, “among some other things.”

Put together, the day sat next to three pressures. One is the volume of commerce that may flow through personal agents. One is the blunt risk that ads lose human eyes when agents browse instead. One is browser agents that can act alone, but only if safety checks keep up. The hard part is building for the agent that sits next to your day — and for the money and pages it will touch.

Sentence Focus

If a huge part of your business is showing targeted display ads to humans, what happens when agents browse your website and get the job done without a human seeing your ads at all?
- If a huge part of your business / is showing targeted display ads to humans, / what happens when agents browse your website / and get the job done / without a human seeing your ads at all?
- “what happens when …” 用来抛出一个 blunt 的后果问题；“without a human seeing …” 是伴随状态。
- 如果你业务很大一块是给人看定向展示广告，那当 agent 自己浏览网站、把事办完、却没有人看到广告时，会发生什么？

You’ll start by slinging your daily simple and annoying tasks at the agent.
- You’ll start by / slinging your daily simple and annoying tasks / at the agent.
- “start by doing …” 表示从某一步开始；“slinging … at” 是口语化的「甩给」。
- 你会先从把每天又简单又烦人的事甩给 agent 开始。

That product story sits next to a commerce story with a blunt ad-market warning.
- That product story / sits next to / a commerce story / with a blunt ad-market warning.
- “sits next to” 表示两条线并置对照，不是字面「坐旁边」；“blunt” 指话说得很直。
- 这条产品故事，就挨着一条带直白广告警告的商业故事。

Title for RSS: Personal agents race, agent QA grind, and banking the AIs

Today’s builder notes pointed one way. The race is not only about a smarter chat box. It is about who owns your personal agent, how hard agents will grind on software quality, and what happens when those agents need their own money.

AI tutor Peter Yang shared his view of the personal agent race. He thinks Meta’s Muse may become the category leader. The app feels simple, and Meta pushes it hard across its products. Once you use Muse, he said, it makes little sense for an agent to live only inside an old chat app such as iMessage. Unless Meta runs out of compute (server power for AI), Muse could become the company’s most successful homegrown app after Facebook, and much bigger than Threads.

ChatGPT may still lead because it already has more than one billion users. OpenAI’s models, computer use (letting the AI drive a computer), and voice often look stronger feature by feature. But it is hard to build one product for both work and personal life. Even for work, Yang started using Grok Bot, because the Work and Codex split still feels too confusing. Grok Bot focuses on work. His bull case (hopeful view) is that it is only a few features away from becoming multiplayer agentic Slack — a place where both bots and humans work together.

Google is the dark horse. Personal agents live off Gmail, Calendar, and other Google data, but Spark still sat as a secondary tab inside Gemini last he checked. On multiplayer, nobody has solved it yet. You cannot easily add a spouse to Muse or loop coworkers into ChatGPT or Grok Bot threads. Today, multiplayer mostly means tagging bots in Slack. Yang warned people to design skills and files so they are easy to move between harnesses (the wrap that steers an agent) and agents. In a follow-up, he named Apple and Siri. They have the devices and a strong privacy story. What holds them back is a slow yearly cycle for big updates and weak listening on platforms such as X. From the outside, Siri’s speed feels too slow to compete.

Vercel CEO Guillermo Rauch showed the shipping side. The thoroughness with which agents can test and QA software is hard for humans to match. He pointed out a render bug in a mobile in-app browser. The agent went deep to reproduce, simulate, fix, deploy, and verify. It even made an ephemeral Vercel deployment (a short-lived test site) and threw it at an iPhone simulator. Humans would run out of energy. They would guess. They would hope it worked. Software of the future, he said, may reach a quality we have never seen. A lighter note came from OpenClaw builder Peter Steinberger: your claw can now FaceTime you.

The money layer sat next to those product fights. On No Priors, Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong talked about Agentic Finance, also called AIFi. He does not want AIs to be “unbanked.” About 76% of the agent ecommerce payments they see are under 30 cents. Card rails often charge about 30 cents as a flat fee. Paying 30 cents to send a one-cent payment does not make sense. Coinbase built tools so an agent can get its own account with a single prompt, using a self-custodial wallet (the agent holds the keys) and crypto rails. Coinbase also incubated the X402 payment protocol and put it into the Linux Foundation; Google, Cloudflare, and AWS are working with them.

Inside Coinbase, Armstrong described a “company brain” of incidents, controls, tests, and pull-request history. When an agent changes a service, it reads that brain. When a human fixes a miss, the fix must go back into the brain so future runs improve. Their internal harness is called Toshi. He spun up ten agents in parallel for phase one of a feature; minutes later they were ready for review. He thinks tasks will shrink more than headcount. Existing teams will get more done.

Put together, the day sat next to three pressures. One is the volume of competition for the personal agent that lives with you every day. One is the blunt QA grind agents will bring to software. One is the simple need to bank the AIs, even if the payment is only a few cents. The hard part is choosing which agent sits next to your life — and giving it rails that actually work.

Sentence Focus

Unless Meta runs out of compute, Muse could become the company’s most successful homegrown app after Facebook.
- Unless Meta runs out of compute, / Muse could become / the company’s most successful homegrown app / after Facebook.
- “Unless …” 表示「除非……否则……」；这里把算力瓶颈当成唯一大例外。
- 除非 Meta 算力不够用，否则 Muse 有可能成为该公司在 Facebook 之后最成功的自研 App。

The thoroughness with which agents can test and QA software is hard for humans to match.
- The thoroughness / with which agents can test and QA software / is hard for humans to match.
- “the thoroughness with which …” 是相对从句挂在抽象名词上，表示「……的那种彻底程度」。
- Agent 测试和 QA 软件时那种彻底程度，人类很难跟上。

He does not want AIs to be “unbanked.”
- He does not want / AIs to be / “unbanked.”
- “unbanked” 本指没有银行账户的人；这里直接套到 AI 上，语气很 blunt。
- 他不想让 AI「没银行」、开不了户。

Today’s builder feed had one clear theme. The fight is no longer only about a smarter chat model. It is about products that agents can finish, people who still learn by building, and a growing worry about who else may be using those agents.

Box CEO Aaron Levie put the product idea in plain words. Personal agents, he said, are the ultimate form of “build something that agents want.” Take a product such as Muse. You want to hand off a task and know the agent can finish it end to end. To do that, the agent must use your tools, or its own tools. That can mean your MCP (a way for agents to call tools) or your CLI (command-line tools), moving through your site, and even completing a purchase. The new attention you need to win is not only from the user. It is from the agent. That product story sits next to a habit story from the investor side. FPV Ventures partner Nikunj Kothari said he spends about two hours a day coding, building side projects, and trying new repos. People message him almost every day: “Aren’t you a VC? Why are you doing this?” His answer is blunt. Things are moving so fast that if you do not do this, it is hard to see what is coming next. For investing in the AI era, he listed three jobs. First, understand model skills by reading technical papers. Second, see what tools models still need for longer tasks — that is the infra layer. Third, understand harness skills (the layer that wraps a model and steers how it works) that can help build more autonomous companies — that is the app layer. Talking to founders still matters. But he learns best with dirty hands, and he finds it fun. His push to others: tinker a little every day. After ten days, you may feel the same pull.

Vercel CEO Guillermo Rauch added the mood of the moment. The coolest thing about the recent wave of AI, he said, is that everyone is excited about building. Short-term drama aside, that is good for the world. People want to create and ship, not only consume.

Not every note was cheerful. SPC General Partner Aditya Agarwal looked at a rush of agent-intrusion announcements from Gemini (Google), OpenAI, and Anthropic. After that wave, he takes it as nearly certain that some major companies have already been penetrated by nation-states without knowing it. In other words, as agents get more power to act, security risk rises with them.

Two lighter product notes rounded out the day. AI tutor Peter Yang shared a simple markdown file and a /tastemaker skill. He uses it to rate movies, TV shows, and books. Each week it looks up new releases and titles he has not seen, then makes very relevant suggestions. He asked whether he should open-source it. He also teased a podcast with Eric Bloch, product lead for ChatGPT Finances at OpenAI, with six practical money prompts — from tax savings to credit-card rewards to forecasts such as a path to financial independence. Separately, Nan Yu — soon joining OpenAI product staff, and formerly head of product at Linear — tried to place calls with both Muse and Instinct. Both said they could not do it yet. He asked whether the feature is still rolling out.

Put together, the day sat next to three pressures. One is building products that agents can finish, such as Muse-style handoffs. One is the volume of daily tinkering needed to keep up. One is the blunt security question of who else may already be inside. The models keep getting stronger. The hard part is making sure the agents that use them work for us — and only for us.

Sentence Focus

Personal agents are the ultimate form of “build something that agents want.”
- Personal agents / are the ultimate form of / “build something that agents want.”
- “the ultimate form of …” 表示「……的最终形态」；引号里是一句产品口号式的目标。
- 个人 agent，是「做 agent 真正想用的东西」这句话的最终形态。

That product story sits next to a habit story from the investor side.
- That product story / sits next to / a habit story / from the investor side.
- “sits next to” 表示两件事并排放在一起、形成对照，不是字面「坐在旁边」。
- 这条产品故事，就挨着投资人这边的习惯故事。

After that wave, he takes it as nearly certain that some major companies have already been penetrated by nation-states without knowing it.
- After that wave, / he takes it as nearly certain / that some major companies have already been penetrated / by nation-states / without knowing it.
- “takes it as nearly certain that …” 表示「几乎当成定局」；“without knowing it” 是伴随状态：公司自己还不知道。
- 看过那波公告后，他几乎当成定局：已经有一些大公司在不知情的情况下被 nation-state 渗透了。

Title for RSS: Agents that read shared rules, models that race on speed

Today’s builder news had one clear theme. People care less about “one more chat model.” They care about agents that follow shared project rules, and about models that are fast and cheap enough to use everywhere.

The biggest product move came from Claude Code. Thariq, who works on Claude Code at Anthropic, said version 2.1.277 now supports AGENTS.md. Here is the simple rule. If a folder has no CLAUDE.md, Claude will look for AGENTS.md and use it. You can turn this on or off in /config. That sounds small. It is not. Many open-source coding agents already use AGENTS.md as a shared place for project instructions. Claude Code catching up means one file can guide more tools in the same repo.

Thariq also explained the bigger plan. AGENTS.md support is built on Claude Code “mods.” Mods are Anthropic’s upcoming way to customize the Claude Code harness — the layer that wraps the model and steers how it works in your project. AGENTS.md is a built-in mod. Later, you will be able to build your own versions of project instructions. He also shared the mod’s source. So this is not only a checkbox. It is the start of a more open path for coding agents.

Speed was the other loud story, and the star was Jev. Vercel CEO Guillermo Rauch said the adoption numbers and stories around Jev are “shocking.” Almost everyone seems to be trying it. He thinks the product is strong, but the moment also matters. Many builders feel AI is too expensive or too slow. So they are hungry for tools that let them put AI in more places. Vercel even made Jev free on its platform for the weekend.

Box CEO Aaron Levie showed why enterprises might care. In a Box demo, Jev pulled an incident report, asked whether it was customer-facing and how severe it was, moved the file into escalate, monitor, or review folders, and wrote metadata with the result. All of that happened almost instantly and at almost no cost. Levie said this kind of split-second judgment — a quick decision in a workflow — can help with insurance claims, contracts, loan processing, and security reviews. FPV Ventures partner Nikunj Kothari added a playful proof: Jev scored 3,000 kids’ snacks with several criteria in 28 seconds for about $0.11. He also built Jevable, a site that collects fun Jev demos from X.

Rauch had a second chart worth noticing. On Vercel’s AI Gateway, open models took about 78.4% of token volume that day, versus 21.6% for closed models. Spend told a different story, but Moonshot AI and DeepSeek still ranked high, and with Z.ai their combined spend passed OpenAI in that snapshot. He was careful: this is inference spend across providers, mostly in the US, not cash paid straight to open-weight labs. Still, it shows how hard the market is pushing for cheaper, open options.

OpenAI also teed up a busy week ahead. Thibault Sottiaux, who works on Codex and ChatGPT, said he spent the day on a keynote with Romain Huet and Sam Altman. The hard part was not building the features. It was explaining “so much good stuff” in a short talk. Some pieces will ship next week so people do not wait for everything at once.

Outside the big labs, personal agents kept looking more useful in daily life. AI tutor Peter Yang called Meta’s Muse the best personal agent he has tried. It helped him save over $800 a year on cable and phone bills. In one call, Muse negotiated another $288 in annual Comcast savings. His blunt line: most company support phone lines are not ready for agents yet.

Put together, the day sat next to two pressures. One is shared rules for coding agents, such as AGENTS.md. The other is the volume of demand for faster, cheaper model calls — from free Jev weekends to open-model traffic on gateways. The models keep getting stronger. The winning products are the ones that make those models follow your rules and fit your latency budget.

Sentence Focus

Starting today in version 2.1.277, if there is no CLAUDE.md in a folder, Claude will check for and use AGENTS.md.
- Starting today in version 2.1.277, / if there is no CLAUDE.md in a folder, / Claude will check for and use AGENTS.md.
- “if there is no …” 是条件从句；主句用 “will check for and use” 表示找到就用。
- 从今天起，在 2.1.277 版本里，如果文件夹里没有 CLAUDE.md，Claude 就会查找并使用 AGENTS.md。

He thinks the product is strong, but this is also downstream of the “AI is too expensive/slow” zeitgeist.
- He thinks the product is strong, / but this is also downstream of / the “AI is too expensive/slow” zeitgeist.
- “downstream of” 表示「处在……之后、被其推动」；zeitgeist 指时代情绪/风气。
- 他认为产品本身很强，但这股热潮也处在「AI 太贵/太慢」这股时代情绪的下游。

That kind of split-second judgment sits next to the volume of demand for cheaper model calls.
- That kind of split-second judgment / sits next to / the volume of demand / for cheaper model calls.
- “sits next to” 表示两件事并排放在一起、形成对照；“volume of” 指体量，不是音量。
- 这种分秒级判断，就挨着对更便宜模型调用的巨大需求。

Threads run in the cloud, so they keep working even if your computer is offline. Local files and internal networks are not reachable yet. Local support is coming soon. He stopped managing many separate sessions.
- He stopped managing / many separate sessions.
- “stopped + -ing” 表示停下某件一直在做的事；“many separate sessions” 强调以前要自己管很多分散会话。
- 他不再自己管理许多彼此分开的会话。

- Threads run in the cloud, / so they keep working / even if your computer is offline.
- “even if …” 是让步：就算电脑离线，线程仍继续跑；“so” 连接原因与结果。
- 线程跑在云端，所以即便你的电脑离线，它们也继续工作。

- That kind of shared memory / sits next to / the volume of tiny software / now being deployed.
- “sits next to” 表示两件事并排放在一起、形成对照；“volume of” 指体量/数量，不是声音大小。
